To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the term ‘traditional masculinity’, when deployed uncritically, carries meanings that are incongruous with critical understandings both of ‘tradition’ as well as ‘masculinity’, and 2) the term ‘masculinity’ should not be equated with ‘traditional masculinity’.

‘traditional masculinity’ can be understood as a socially constructed and multiple set of practices and beliefs, which is not synonymous with hegemonic masculinity and which can be used in ways that are congruent with critical perspectives on tradition and masculinity.
‘traditional masculinity’ as a term has multiple, diverse, and often conflicting meanings; it is socially constructed and not universal; and it is not the same as hegemonic masculinity.

how we can rethink ‘traditional masculinity’ so as to make it a more useful concept within the critical literature on gender.
the ways in which the term ‘traditional masculinity’, as it is currently used, is both conceptually problematic and potentially problematic in terms of the politics of gender.
the meanings of ‘traditional masculinity’ and the ways in which it has been used in research on gender and masculinities.

‘traditional masculinity’ has a complex and contradictory relationship with both tradition and hegemonic masculinity, and that the concept needs to be more carefully theorized and deployed in critical gender research.
